title: A contact path for a nonprofit
metaTitle: A nonprofit contact page that replies
excerpt: Separate help, volunteering, gifts, and concerns. Say who replies, how soon, and what to have ready. A ten-field form mixes intents and loses people.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, for a piece on making each way to write look separate.
caption: Poppies against a clear sky, each one distinct. Contact paths should be that separate. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why split a nonprofit contact page into doors?
faqs.answer: Because the intents are different. A person seeking intake, a volunteer, a donor with an unusual gift, and someone with a concern should not share one essay box. Each door can name who replies and what to have ready. Ordinary gifts should go to the giving page, not into a please contact me form.

faqs.question: What response time should you publish?
faqs.answer: The one you already keep. Different doors can have different windows. If the inbox is read on Mondays, say Mondays. A same-day promise copied from a template will be broken, and the person who needed help will remember the break.

faqs.question: Should sensitive details go in the form?
faqs.answer: No. Ask people not to send a full case history through the website, and tell them where the in-person or safer setting is. The form is for routing. The program page should already show hours and address so people do not have to write you for the basics.

markdown:
A nonprofit contact page tells a donor or a participant what happens after they reach out, how soon, and what to have ready. The real actions are still to give, join, or read the program. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them, and so is a single inbox that mixes a person seeking help with a person offering a sponsorship.

Write the page as a handoff between intents. Someone in need, someone who wants to volunteer, someone who wants to give, someone who has a concern. They should not all be poured into "tell us about yourself." Name the doors. Then make each door short.

## Separate the intents

The first screen should offer the paths you actually staff. Apply or get help. Volunteer. Give. Press or partnerships, if those are real and answered. A concern. Four or five links with a sentence each will outperform one generic form, because the sentence tells the visitor they have been expected.

Word the help path in the language of the program. "Ask about Tuesday intake" is clearer than "general inquiry." If the help path should not be an email at all, say so. "Intake is in person, Tuesdays 4 to 7, at this address. The form is for people who need directions or an accommodation, not for a decision on a case." That sentence prevents the wrong tool from being used, and it respects people who are about to share something sensitive.

The give path should usually be the giving page, not a form that says "I would like to donate, please contact me." Send them to the amount, the designation, and the receipt. Use the contact page for gifts that do not fit the form: a pledge, a donor-advised fund, a question about a restriction. Say that plainly so ordinary gifts do not detour through an inbox.

The volunteer path should restate the boundary in miniature. The commitment, the check, the next session. Then a short form or a link to the information night. Enthusiasm without the boundary produces a list of people you will disappoint. The contact page is a fine place to repeat the boundary in two lines.

## What happens next, and what to have ready

Under each path, say the handoff. Who reads it, what the first reply contains, and the window you keep. "The intake coordinator replies within two business days and will tell you whether to come Tuesday or which partner fits better." "The volunteer lead replies with the next orientation date." "Finance replies about non-standard gifts once a week." Different windows are fine. Hidden windows are not.

Publish only windows you meet. If the true answer is "we read this inbox on Mondays," say Mondays. A promise of same-day care, copied from a startup template, will be broken and will be remembered. The contact page is an operations page. Marketing does not get to invent a faster organization than the one you have.

Say what to have ready, and keep it short. For help: the program they mean, the best way to reach them, and any access need. For volunteering: the role and the days they can keep. For a non-standard gift: the vehicle and the timing. Ask them not to include sensitive details that should be said in person, and tell them where the in-person setting is. A web form is a poor place for a full case history. Guide people toward the safer setting without making them feel turned away.

If a program page already answers the question, link it beside the form. Hours, address, cost, eligibility. Many people open "contact" because they could not find the fact. Give them the fact. The form remains for what the page cannot know. A contact page that withholds the address until someone writes is an obstacle disguised as a relationship.

## A short form for each door

Each form should match its intent. Help: name, contact, program, a short message, an access note. Volunteer: name, contact, role, days. Gift exception: name, contact, the kind of gift. Concern: name if they want to give it, contact, the program, what happened. Do not ask all of these of all people. A universal form is how you get ten fields.

Leave off the research. How did you hear about us, job title, household income, interest checkboxes for your newsletter. If you need a mailing list, ask after the reply, as its own question, defaulting to no. A person seeking help did not arrive to become an audience segment. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) includes understandable input: labels, instructions, and help recovering from errors. That standard is also simple kindness. Label every field in text that stays put. When a field is wrong, say so beside it and keep the rest of what they typed.

Required fields should be the ones without which you cannot reply. A way to reach them, and enough to know which door. Everything else can be optional. Mark optional fields as optional. People in a hurry will assume every box is a gate. On success, repeat what will happen and the window. On failure, do not clear the form. Test both states on a phone.

Spam protection should be quiet. A puzzle that blocks a tired person, or a script that rejects common email domains, will be felt as "they did not want to hear from me." Choose a method a human can pass. Then check that real messages are not landing in a junk folder nobody opens. The technical success of a form is that a person reads it.

## Routing and the human inbox

Each door needs an owner and a backup. Write the owners down internally, and write the roles on the page. When the owner is out, the backup reads the same inbox. A shared inbox with no duty roster is how messages age. Review it on a schedule that matches the window you published. If you promised two business days, the review cadence has to beat two business days.

Existing participants and current donors often need a different door from new ones. A question about a case, a receipt, a failed recurring gift. Give them a path that does not look like a first-time application. Otherwise urgent notes wait behind new inquiries, and new inquiries wait behind emergencies. Two sentences and two addresses, or one form with a first question that routes, will do. The routing has to be real in the inbox, not only visual on the page.

Publishing a phone number is a promise that the number behaves like the page. Answered, or returned in the stated window, by someone who can speak to the program. A number that rings in an empty office is a second broken form. If you cannot staff it, publish the hours of the desk you do staff, and make the form the path the rest of the time. Say that. People forgive a closed phone. They do not forgive a phone that pretends to be open.

An address in text belongs on this page even if it is also on the program page. Visits, mail, and deliveries depend on it. Note whether you welcome unannounced visits. Many programs do not, for good reasons. "Please come during intake hours" is a boundary that protects staff and participants. Write it without apology and without scare language.

## Concerns, privacy, and the tone of the reply

A concern path should not be cheerful. It should be specific. Who reads it, whether it can be anonymous, and what the person can expect. A board email or a named role outside the program being criticized is often the right destination. Publishing it is a sign that you have imagined being wrong. Hiding it is a sign you have not.

Privacy copy should say what happens to a message. Used to reply and to deliver the program. Not sold. Not dropped into a newsletter because they asked for help. If a message might contain sensitive information, say how long you keep it and who on staff can see it, in a sentence a person can finish. Point to the longer policy. Do not make the policy a gate in front of the form.

Staff replies should be able to say no. The program is full. The request sits outside the boundary. Here is the better-matched organization, if you truly know one. A contact path that can only say yes will either overpromise or go silent. Silence is the crueler no. Put the permission to decline in the internal instructions, and make the public boundary accurate so fewer declines are needed.

## The page around the forms

Give a new visitor one clear picture of the organization above the doors. What you do, where, and the link to the program. They may have landed here from search without seeing anything else. Do not make them pass a newsletter modal to reach the doors. Do not lead with a donation plea on a page a participant opened in distress. The doors come first. A gift link can be one of the doors, labeled as a gift.

Keep facts identical to the program page and the footer. Hours, address, the response window. Inconsistencies look like neglect, and neglect is the fear both donors and participants arrive with. Read the three surfaces together when you change a season's hours. The contact page is the one people trust last, so it hurts most when it is the stale one.

Hanabi builds the path as part of the site, with forms you can edit, in the repository, rather than a plugin the next staff member is afraid to open. The client portal can hold the routing notes next to the program sheets so a new coordinator can see who reads which door. The public page stays short. The operations live where staff can find them.

## Try every door

Before you announce the page, send a message through each door, from a phone. Help, volunteer, odd gift, concern. Confirm the right person received it, the auto-reply matched the door, and the human reply matched the window and the boundary. Fix the leaks. Then delete any field that did not change the reply. The form should feel smaller after the test, not larger.

Ask a participant, if you can do it ethically and without burden, or ask a front-desk volunteer who remembers being new. Have them find how to ask for help starting from the homepage on a phone. If they hesitate, the label is wrong or the form is long. Change the label. Cut the field. Do not add a paragraph of explanation above a confusing control. Explanation is how confusing controls survive.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) when you want this handoff designed with the rest of the site. Bring the inboxes you really read and the windows you really keep. The page should describe that organization, not a faster imaginary one.

Once the doors work, look at what still should not be on the site at all. [What not to put on the site for a nonprofit](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-nonprofit) is the next piece, because a sad photograph and a lone donate button will keep confusing the people these doors were built to welcome.
